title: Regional spike widths added prediction value at a 0.35 ms class boundary but little at 0.45 ms
abstract: We tested whether regional mean spike width can be predicted from narrow-unit fractions and fixed global class means. We used 63,176 IBL units in 190 candidate regions and all 462 equal splits of 12 labs. At the source study boundary of 0.35 ms, 71 to 96 regions met both-class count rules per split. Regional class means reduced median error by 26.1% against fractions alone and won in every split. Narrow and broad mean widths repeated across lab groups, with median correlations of 0.689 and 0.699. Added gain fell to 8.1% at 0.40 ms and 0.5% at 0.45 ms. With a fixed eligible cohort across thresholds, gains were 29.9% at 0.35 ms and -2.8% at 0.45 ms. With equal session weights, the primary gain was 18.6% and the full model won in 427 of 462 splits. A fitted fraction-only line did not remove the primary gain. These results show useful width information within the source study bins, but they do not support a boundary-independent split of composition and intrinsic width. Width bins are not molecular cell types. We supply regional class-conditioned summaries, code, full split scores and exact source hashes. Split ranges are not confidence limits; no causal effect of wiring or genes is estimated.

display.caption: Prediction errors and repeatability at 0.35 ms, with gain across four class boundaries. Bars on the right show split percentiles, not confidence limits.
